chapters.title: The Slot Machine In Your Pocket

beats.text: This is me paying forty dollars a month to a dating app so I can stay single.
Zero new matches. Same as last month. Same as the month before that.
And here's the twist. The app is not broken. It's working exactly like it was built to.
Because me finding love was never the goal. Me still paying is the goal.
By the end of this video you'll know the one move that makes a dating app lose money on you and it costs zero dollars.
But most people swipe away before that part which is exactly what the app wants.
So let me tell you how this started. My friend says just download Tinder bro. It's free.
And I'm not gonna lie I felt smart. Free app. Free love. What could go wrong?
Free. Remember that word.
Week one I swipe on everyone. I swipe on the bus. I swipe in the shower. I swipe while my mom is talking to me.
I swiped so much my thumb started hurting. I had a swiping injury. I almost went to a doctor.
Me swiping right on every single person within fifty miles.
Zero matches. So the app pops up a little message. Want to see who already likes you? Just upgrade.
And I think wait. People already like me? I pay. Obviously.
I paid so fast my card didn't even have time to be scared. Forty dollars. Gone. For a list of people who like me.
Turns out the people who liked me were a guy named Steve and a bot selling sunglasses.
Me after paying to see who likes me.
So I get mad and delete Tinder and download Hinge instead. New app. Fresh start. Different company.
Except it's not. Tinder and Hinge and Match and OkCupid and Plenty of Fish are all owned by the same company.
One company and a bunch of logos. It's like a restaurant that changes its sign every night but the same guy is cooking.
It's like storming out of one supermarket because you hate it and walking into a different aisle of the same supermarket.
So when I switch apps to escape one subscription I'm still paying the exact same people.
It's like breaking up with someone and then dating their twin. Who also has your credit card.
Me switching dating apps.
And then it hit me. If I meet someone tomorrow and delete the app what does the app make off me? Basically nothing.
But if I stay single and keep swiping and keep paying every single month? Now I'm a great customer.
Think about it from their side. Every month I'm sad and single is a month they get paid. My loneliness is their rent money.
A happy couple who deletes the app is a lost customer. A sad guy who keeps swiping is a subscription.
The dating app business plan.
To be fair the apps don't want everyone sad forever. Some people really do find love. They just make more money from the ones who don't.
Think about a gym that loses money when you get fit. Or a dentist who loses money when your teeth are fine. Weird right?
And here's the part that really got me. The notification that says someone likes you? It isn't always a person.
The FTC sued Match Group and said the company sent people those someone likes you emails from accounts it had already flagged as likely fake. To get people to pay.
So the app was basically catfishing me into paying. With its own fake people.
Me getting excited about a like from a fake account.
In twenty twenty five Match agreed to pay fourteen million dollars to settle and it didn't admit doing anything wrong.
Fourteen million sounds like a lot. For a company that big it's like you or me paying a parking ticket.
So that little buzz in your pocket? It's not a love letter. It's a sales email.
Me after learning that.
So what does my forty dollars actually buy?
I get to see who liked me. Unlimited swipes. An undo button. And a boost so more people see my face.
And the boost is a little auction. The more people pay to be seen the more you have to pay to be seen too.
And there's an even fancier version that costs more. For people who want to be single at a premium level.
None of that finds me a better person. It just removes a little wall the app built in the first place.
It's like a guy who builds a toll booth in the middle of your street and then sells you a pass to skip it.
Paying to fix a problem the app made.
And most people never pay a cent. They're the free version. The bait. The faces people like me pay to see.
And here's why I kept opening it. Swiping feels like a slot machine.
Most swipes get nothing. Nothing. Nothing. Then boom. A match. And my brain goes crazy.
Scientists tried this on pigeons. Give them food every time and they get bored. Give them food at random and they peck that button all day.
I am the pigeon. You are the pigeon. We are all pecking the button at two in the morning.
Psychologists call that a random reward. Same trick as casinos and same trick as your social media feed.
Las Vegas figured this out a long time ago. Dating apps just put the casino in your pocket.
Me checking the app for the twentieth time today.
Be honest. You've checked an app like that in the bathroom at work. We all have.
And even when I finally got a date? That costs money too now.
Dinner and drinks and the Uber and the haircut I got for the date. One night cost me almost two hundred dollars.
The haircut alone was forty dollars. For a guy who looks exactly the same after.
And she ordered the lobster. On a first date. I respect it but my bank account doesn't.
My bank account after one date.
Meanwhile my dad took my mom to a diner for two burgers and a milkshake. They've been married thirty years.
Thirty years. On a milkshake. And I spent two hundred dollars to get ghosted by text.
No wonder so many people my age say dating just doesn't feel worth the money anymore. A lot of us just stopped spending.
And it's not because we don't want love. It's because rent already eats our paycheck and love wants a bite too.
And you know what? Some of them are winning. About half of Gen Z says they spend zero dollars a month on dating.
They watch a movie at home. They cook pasta. And somehow they still fall in love.
So here's how I date now. Quick reminder this is education and not relationship advice.
First I use the free version. Most of my real matches happened without paying a single cent.
The paid stuff mostly makes you feel like you're doing something. Like buying running shoes instead of running.
I did the free version for a month and got more dates than when I was paying. Because I stopped swiping on everyone and actually read the profiles.
Second I move off the app fast. The app's job is done the second we swap numbers. So I swap numbers.
Phone call first. Ten minutes. If it's weird on the phone it's going to be weird at a two hundred dollar dinner.
Dating apps when two people swap numbers.
Third if a whole month goes by with zero real conversations I cancel. I don't upgrade. I cancel.
Set the rule before you start. One month. If nothing real happens the money stays in my pocket.
And fourth cheap dates work. A coffee or a walk tells you more about a person than a lobster ever will.
Me asking her on a walk instead of a fancy dinner.
Also a walk has no lobster on the menu. Just saying.
So here's the one move. Get off the app as fast as you can. Every day you stay is money for them.
The app makes money while I'm swiping. The second I'm on a real date it makes nothing.
Every hour you spend talking to a real human is an hour the app can't sell to you.
The app watching us leave together.
The best way to beat a dating app is to stop needing it.
Oh and that bot selling sunglasses? Still messages me every week. Most loyal relationship I've ever had.
Next time my sister tells me a kid costs three hundred thousand dollars. I laugh. Then I do the math.
Subscribe. It's free. And unlike dating apps it actually stays free.
